cim_eredeti: Artificial intelligence and law: how AI is transforming legal practice
szoveg_eredeti:
According to Thomson Reuters’ 2026 AI in Professional Services report, 41% of law firms surveyed worldwide are already using generative AI, nearly twice as many as a year earlier. This technology is changing how lawyers conduct research, analyze contracts, and prepare legal strategies.

However, 64% of legal professionals surveyed in five European countries, including Spain, by Karnov Group a company specializing in legal information and technology, believe there is a high or very high risk that younger professionals will fail to develop sufficient legal skills because of their use of AI. This finding highlights the need to combine technology with professional judgment.

For students nearing the end of their law degree who plan to practice law, programs such as Esade’s Spanish-language Máster Universitario en Abogacía y Procura + Máster de Especialización combine the use of legal AI tools with highly specialized training, teaching and assessment redesigned for the AI era and the development of essential professional skills.

But how is AI transforming the practice of law, and what applications and risks should future lawyers understand? We explore these questions below.

AI in the legal profession encompasses technologies that can process information, identify patterns, and generate content to support legal work. Generative AI has expanded these capabilities by enabling interaction through natural language.

However, AI in the legal field complements rather than replaces legal reasoning. Interpreting laws and defending a client’s interests still require professional judgment.

As we explain in our article on AI for lawyers in Spain, this technology speeds up tasks and streamlines complex legal processes. Its use is already widespread: according to the White Paper on Artificial Intelligence and Law published by the Spanish General Council of Lawyers, 60% of legal professionals in Spain already use AI-powered applications.

International reports identify similar tasks as the main applications of AI. Thomson Reuters’ 2025 Generative AI in Professional Services report identifies document review and summarization, legal research, and the drafting of legal documents and contracts as the leading applications. LexisNexis’s The AI-Dependent Lawyer survey of 543 legal professionals in the UK points to the same trends.

In corporate legal departments, AI is used primarily for contract management. Consulting firm Gartner identifies six key applications: extracting data from contracts, automating contract reviews, analyzing contractual risks, summarizing legal documents, receiving and classifying internal inquiries, and transcribing and summarizing meetings.

Adoption is also growing rapidly. According to a survey by the Association of Corporate Counsel and Everlaw, active use of generative AI among surveyed in-house lawyers in the United States rose from 23% to 52% in one year.

AI raises new legal questions, from data protection to liability for automated decisions. Future lawyers will need to understand the regulations governing the development and use of these technologies.

In the European Union, the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) establishes obligations based on the risk posed by AI systems. For example, it classifies certain systems that assist judicial authorities in interpreting and applying the law to specific cases as high-risk.

Since February 2025, it has also required organizations that use AI systems in their professional activities, including law firms and legal advisory firms, to promote AI literacy among their staff.

In addition, Spain’s Digital Omnibus adopted in 2026 (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) has amended some of the AI Act’s requirements and postponed certain obligations for high-risk systems, making it important to keep track of the implementation timeline.

In Spain, the General Council of the Judiciary also approved Instruction 2/2026 in January 2026 on the use of AI in judicial proceedings. It establishes limits and requires human control over judicial decisions.

A common question among lawyers is: “What are the legal risks of using AI?”One of the main risks is hallucinations: seemingly reliable responses that contain fabricated information, such as nonexistent laws, fictitious case law, or incorrect legal interpretations.

The consequences have already become apparent in the courts. In July 2026, the High Court of Justice of Galicia fined a lawyer €1,800 for submitting an appeal drafted using AI that contained 24 fabricated or inconsistent legal citations.

In other words, legal professionals need to learn about technology (what it is and how it works), how to use it effectively, how to apply it judiciously and when not to use it, and how to understand and respond to its implications through governance and regulation. Rather than mastering a particular tool that may become obsolete within months, the decisive skill will be learning how to learn.

AI is also creating new opportunities for specialization in areas such as technology regulation, data protection, and advising on intelligent systems, expanding the traditional career paths available to law graduates.

If you are nearing the end of your law degree and want to practice law, choosing a master’s program that prepares you for the profession, offers specialized training, and incorporates new technologies can make a difference at the start of your legal career.

Esade’s Spanish-language Máster Universitario en Abogacía y Procura + Máster de Especialización brings these three elements together through a dual degree and a hands-on approach to learning based on simulated litigation, designed to develop the skills required by the profession.

Both solutions give students hands-on experience with the technologies transforming legal practice.

But access to these tools is only the starting point. Esade Law School has launched a project to transform its law master’s programs for the AI era, rethinking what students learn, how they are taught, and how they are assessed. Assessment focuses on the learning process, not just the outcome, with greater emphasis on oral arguments, simulations, and real-world cases. Class time focuses on what AI cannot replace: debate, negotiation, judgment, and communication.

AI is transforming the work of law firms by automating repetitive tasks and streamlining processes such as legal research, contract review, and the preparation of legal documents. This allows lawyers to devote more time to higher-value activities, such as strategic advice, negotiation, and defending their clients’ interests.

The main risks include generating incorrect or fabricated legal information, breaching client confidentiality, discriminatory bias, loss of judgment due to overreliance on AI, and failure to comply with legal or professional obligations. To minimize these risks, it is essential to verify AI-generated results and establish protocols that ensure responsible use.
